turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Monday, September 21st. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex — and we're starting in Moscow, because Ukraine just launched its biggest drone strike of the war.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Over 1,000 drones hit Russia overnight Friday into Saturday, hundreds of them aimed at Moscow itself. The mayor called it the largest single attack the capital has ever taken.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What actually got hit?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A Moscow oil refinery and a residential building both took direct damage. This isn't the front-line story we've been tracking around Lyman and the Vivaldi counteroffensive — this is Kyiv proving it can reach the capital at scale, which is a different kind of pressure entirely.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does hitting Moscow directly change Russia's calculus, or just its air-defense budget?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Both, but the more interesting read is symbolic — a thousand-drone raid that residents actually feel in the capital does something a front-line stalemate can't, which is puncture the sense that the war stays comfortably far away for ordinary Russians.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second story — Russia just held an election, technically.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: First wartime parliamentary election in the country's history, voting ran Friday through Sunday. United Russia's sitting on 57.8% with about 93% of the count in.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is anyone treating that number as real?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Not seriously — but the point of the exercise was never the number, it's holding a national vote at all while running an active mobilization, which is its own message about regime confidence.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Third — Germany had two more state elections Saturday, and the fragmentation story just picked up new geography.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Berlin: Die Linke, the far left, won outright at 25.7%, ahead of Merz's own CDU at 18.8%. Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, on the other coast: AfD took the most votes of any party.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the far left wins the capital and the far right wins the northeast, same weekend.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Same weekend, same country, same governing coalition trying to hold the center — that's the story. Germany's two-party postwar system is genuinely gone; what's replacing it depends entirely on which state you're standing in.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Onto US business — and it's the end of an era at Berkshire Hathaway.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Warren Buffett, 96, stepped down as Berkshire's chairman Friday. His letter to shareholders: "Father Time always wins." He becomes chairman emeritus, stays on as a director.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Who takes the chair?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: His son, Howard Buffett — Greg Abel remains CEO, a role he's held since January. So the succession plan that's been telegraphed for years is now fully executed: operating control to Abel, board control to family.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is that split — family holds the board, an outsider runs the company — unusual for a company this size?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's the classic conglomerate solution actually — keep the culture and capital-allocation discipline anchored through family board control while an operator handles the businesses day to day. Whether it survives without Buffett's personal judgment calling the shots on capital allocation is the real multi-year question for Berkshire's valuation.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second business story — a new front just opened in the AI-safety fight.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Friday, a new antitrust suit landed in Northern California district court, alleging Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, and Google DeepMind illegally coordinated to slow down AI development.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the evidence for coordination?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The complaint cites Dario Amodei's essay from September 12th, a same-day public agreement from Altman, Musk, and Hassabis, plus an industry letter from back in July — treating a public convergence of safety rhetoric as evidence of an actual restraint-of-trade agreement.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a genuinely different legal theory than what we usually see in this space.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It is — the normal antitrust story is companies colluding to raise prices or lock out competitors. This complaint inverts it: alleges the labs colluded to slow innovation down, which if it holds up as a theory, means talking publicly about safety risk together could itself become litigation exposure. Worth watching whether a court takes that theory seriously at all.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: International — Nigeria's got two things happening at once.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Dangote's $5 billion refinery IPO — billed as Africa's largest — opened for subscription Saturday. Same week, separately, Nigeria rejoins the FTSE frontier index today.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why does the index re-entry matter on top of the IPO itself?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because it pulls passive index-tracking money into Nigerian equities automatically — Dangote Cement, First HoldCo, and MTN all get that inflow. BUA, UBA, and Seplat are excluded on free-float grounds, so it's a selective re-rating, not a blanket one.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Last one — Argentina, where the IMF is showing up to check the homework.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: An IMF staff mission arrives this week to review reserves, financing risk, and the budget. Household debt just hit a 22-year high, and country risk closed the week at 524, up from 485 — Merval down 2.5% on the week.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a real deterioration, not noise.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Real enough that it's the kind of number an IMF mission specifically exists to interrogate — reserves and financing risk are the two things that turn a debt story into a crisis story if they move the wrong way at the same time.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Markets today are a "check the app" segment on the surface — but there's a real divergence hiding under it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Friday's close: S&P up 0.17%, Nasdaq up 0.39% — both quiet, both green. Dow down 0.18%. On the headline numbers, nothing happened.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: But you said "hiding under it."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Russell 2000, small caps, down half a percent — quiet in isolation, but negative while the mega-cap indices went green, which is the first crack. Then look outside the US entirely: the FTSE dropped 1.51%, the DAX dropped 1.6%, both genuinely major moves.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's driving Europe specifically?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: FTSE — Hormuz tension plus a Bank of England rate-cut-doubt repricing hit banks and energy hard, even with stronger UK retail sales in the same data set. DAX — a quadruple-witching options expiry collided with an autos selloff: Volkswagen down almost 6%, Porsche down 5.2%, Mercedes down 4.8%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So it's not one catalyst, it's technical plus fundamental stacking on the same day.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly, and that's the real story of the week — US large-cap calm is masking genuine stress everywhere else. The 10-year's sitting around 5.01%, basically holding the level we've already flagged, and the Fed's "higher for longer" dot plot is still the backdrop. One more hike penciled in for later this year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Anything on commodities worth a number?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: WTI pulled back 1.58% to $100.30, easing off the Mideast-premium highs from earlier in the week. Gold basically flat, down 0.4%. Everything else — full index levels, the peso, the rest of it — it's all on the Markets tab.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: If the divergence holds, what actually breaks first?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Watch small caps and Europe together, not the S&P. Mega-cap US indices can stay calm on AI-earnings momentum alone for a while — Russell 2000 and European banks are the parts of the market with nowhere to hide if rates genuinely stay elevated into next year.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Our deep dive today isn't markets, and it isn't energy — it's labor economics, and it's about who takes care of billionaires' children.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Where's this from?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Economist's Saturday newsletter — "Nannying for the ultra-rich is increasingly demanding, and lucrative." Elite nanny salaries are now reaching $200,000 a year.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: $200,000, for childcare?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: On an hourly basis, that rivals what an entry-level employee at a major investment fund pulls in — for roughly 12-hour days, seven days a week, in exchange for a full week completely off afterward. Anita Rogers, who runs British American Household Staffing, told the paper that families who used to balk at those numbers are now actively competing for the best candidates.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What does "the best candidate" even look like at that price point?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Elite-academy pedigree, fluency in multiple languages, a degree from a top university, and — this is the part that tells you the real story — documented experience on yachts and private jets, plus a willingness to relocate on essentially no notice.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's not a childcare job description, that's an executive-assistant job description with a kid attached.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's exactly the thesis. What's happening is the ultra-wealthy service economy professionalizing and stratifying the same way finance did decades ago — credentialism, comp structures pegged to scarcity, round-the-clock availability priced as a premium, not an inconvenience.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is this really new, or has domestic staffing for the ultra-rich always worked this way and we're just now reading about the numbers?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Genuinely accelerating, per the agencies quoted — the willingness to pay top dollar is new behavior even among families who've always had staff. It tracks a broader pattern: as wealth concentrates further at the very top, the services built to support that wealth get more specialized, more credentialed, and more expensive, not linearly, but in a winner-take-most way that mirrors what's happened in finance and now, apparently, in childcare.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: It's worth putting next to the other story in this episode — Buffett handing Berkshire's chairmanship to his son.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, that's the connective tissue — whether it's a $200,000 nanny or a trillion-dollar conglomerate, the question of who's trusted to actually tend a fortune, and what that trust costs, is the same question at wildly different scales. The nanny economy is just the version of it playing out in someone's actual household instead of a boardroom.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Does this trend have an obvious ceiling, or does $200,000 keep climbing?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: No obvious ceiling yet, because the constraint isn't the families' willingness to pay — it's the supply of candidates who actually clear that credential bar. As long as ultra-high-net-worth wealth keeps growing faster than that talent pool, the price keeps being bid up, exactly like a scarce asset in any other market.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is there a labor-side story here too, or is it purely a story about the families paying?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There's a real one — a job that used to be seen as informal, often undocumented, low-status work is being pulled into something closer to a proper professional track, with agencies, contracts, and credential requirements. That's arguably better for the people doing it, more transparent pay, clearer hours, even if the underlying reason it's happening is wealth concentration at the very top.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A strange but genuinely revealing way to start the week.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Energy — and there's a real regulatory fight in Virginia over who actually pays for the data-center buildout.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: This is from Utility Dive's Friday Daily Dive. Virginia's State Corporation Commission ordered direct assignment of transmission costs to data centers, instead of socializing those costs across the entire ratepayer base.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's Microsoft's position?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Preserving its right to formally appeal — deadline's November. Dominion Energy, meanwhile, has until October to propose a compliant cost-allocation policy of its own.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And there's a federal angle too.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Same day, the US House passed a ratepayer-protection bill limiting exactly this kind of cost-shifting. ClearView Energy Partners' read is that it would "largely reinforce" a shift that's already underway through state-level large-load tariffs — but it's unlikely to clear the Senate before the midterms eat the calendar.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why does Virginia specifically matter here versus any other state doing this?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because it's the densest data-center market in the country — Northern Virginia, inside PJM. If direct cost-assignment holds up here and spreads, it changes the actual siting math for every hyperscaler deciding where to build next. This is a sharper, more direct test than anything we've covered on the moratorium-audit or loss-of-load side — this is a hyperscaler litigating a utility's cost-allocation methodology directly.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What if Microsoft wins the appeal?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Then the socialized-cost model holds a while longer in Virginia specifically, and every other state watching this case gets a data point that ratepayer-protection efforts can be litigated down. Either outcome sets precedent — that's why it's the lead story, not a footnote.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Anything on the supply side worth a number?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Hitachi is doubling US production of small and medium power transformers — the 10 to 160 MVA range, up to 230 kilovolts — at a Mississippi facility. They're explicitly framing it as easing industry-wide supply constraints.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a concrete data point against the transformer-bottleneck story we've been tracking.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Genuinely concrete — a name, a location, a spec range, not a vague "supply chains are improving" line. It doesn't erase the bottleneck, but it's the clearest single supply-side response we've seen named this specifically.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One more before we move on?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Meta signed a new 144-megawatt solar PPA with Apex Clean Energy in Texas — and Meta's getting exclusive rights to all the environmental attributes and RECs from the project, not just the power itself.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why does the REC exclusivity matter separately from the megawatts?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because RECs are the accounting mechanism hyperscalers use to claim renewable-matched load for their sustainability reporting — locking up all of them, not just buying the power, is what actually lets Meta count this project cleanly against its own targets rather than splitting the environmental credit with someone else.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Anything moving on the financing side, away from the hyperscalers themselves?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: JPMorgan and Santander are leading a £1.1 billion loan for a Drax solar deal in the UK — a reminder that the capital backing this buildout isn't only coming from Big Tech balance sheets, it's also flowing through conventional project-finance banks underwriting renewables at scale. And on the smaller-scale end, Burlington, the retailer, is expanding on-site behind-the-meter solar across distribution-connected sites in Arizona, California, and Georgia.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a genuinely different customer than a hyperscaler campus.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Completely different — corporate BTM adoption is spreading well beyond data centers into ordinary retail footprints, which tells you the economics of behind-the-meter generation have gotten attractive enough to pencil out for a business with nothing to do with AI at all.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Bago tayo pumunta sa Pilipinas, dalawang salita muna — kapwa may kinalaman sa mga balitang pampulitika ngayong araw.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Simulan natin sa "pagpigil."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Pagpigil" — ang ibig sabihin, ang pagtigil o pagsupil sa isang bagay bago pa man ito lumala. Ginagamit ito kapag pinipigilan ng isang tao o awtoridad ang isang posibleng gulo o kaguluhan bago pa man ito mangyari.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: May kaibhan ba ito sa "pagbabawal"?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Oo — ang "pagbabawal" ay tungkol sa isang patakaran o kautusan na nagsasabing bawal ang isang bagay. Ang "pagpigil" naman, mas tungkol sa aktuwal na hakbang o presensiya — ang paglagay ng hadlang para hindi kumalat o lumaki ang isang sitwasyon, kahit hindi ito legal na ipinagbabawal.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Halimbawa?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Naglagay ang pulisya ng dagdag na tauhan bilang pagpigil sa posibleng karahasan." Gagamitin natin ito mamaya, dahil literal itong nangyayari ngayong araw sa Maynila.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Sige, susunod — "pagkakakulong."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Pagkakakulong" — ang kalagayan ng pagiging nakakulong o nakapiit, karaniwang habang naghihintay ng paglilitis o pagdinig. Malimit itong gamitin sa konteksto ng batas — hindi ito basta "pagkabihag," na mas pangkalahatan.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ano'ng pagkakaiba nito sa "pagkabihag"?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ang "pagkabihag," maaaring resulta ng digmaan, aksidente, o kahit sitwasyong hindi legal. Ang "pagkakakulong," espesipikong tumutukoy sa opisyal, legal na pagpigil sa kalayaan ng isang tao habang may kaso o utos ng korte.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Halimbawa naman ng gamit?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "Nanatili sa pagkakakulong ang dating pangulo habang naghihintay ng pagsisimula ng kanyang paglilitis." Gagamitin din natin ito sa susunod na segment.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Mayroon bang pagkakatulad sa dating ng dalawang salita, kahit magkaiba ang konteksto?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Oo — pareho silang tungkol sa pagpapanatili ng kontrol sa isang mapanganib o hindi tiyak na sitwasyon, isa sa lansangan, isa sa loob ng bilangguan. Kapag pinagsabay mo sa isang balita, makikita mo kung gaano kaingat ang paraan ng pagpapanatili ng kaayusan sa bansa ngayong araw.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ngayong araw, ika-54 na anibersaryo ng deklarasyon ng batas militar ni Marcos Sr. noong 1972 — at bilang pagpigil sa posibleng karahasan, isinara ang Malacañang complex, may mahigit 17,000 pulis na naka-alerto sa buong Metro Manila.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Bakit ganito kalaki ang seguridad ngayong taon?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Dahil sa nangyari noong nakaraang taon — nagulo ang isang rally laban sa katiwalian sa Mendiola, isang patay, daan-daang sugatan, 216 arestado. Ngayon, magtitipon ang mga grupo sa Liwasang Bonifacio bago maglakad patungong Mendiola Peace Arch, may mga barrier na nakalagay bago pa man magsimula.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In English — this is a preemptive security posture, not a reaction to anything happening yet, specifically because last year's rally got hijacked into a riot. Traffic's rerouted around the whole route.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Meanwhile, sa Hague — nanatili sa pagkakakulong si dating Pangulong Duterte matapos ang kanyang unang personal na pagharap sa ICC sa loob ng halos labingwalong buwan.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What actually happened at that hearing?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A fitness-to-stand-trial hearing, September 16th. Trial Chamber III confirmed the trial itself opens November 30th, on the drug-war killings case. Judges denied his release specifically citing flight and interference risk now that the trial date is set.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's a separate track from the domestic impeachment case entirely.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Completely separate — this is the international ICC track. And judges also ordered prosecutors to trim the evidentiary record, which is currently 324,000 pages and 193 hours of testimony, before trial actually starts.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's an enormous amount of material to compress in two months.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which tells you the trial itself, once it starts, is going to move fast by ICC standards — the judges are clearly not interested in letting the volume of evidence become its own delay tactic.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's happening with the other big legal story — Romualdez?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: His lawyers told the Sandiganbayan's Third Division he'll seek bail, even though plunder is non-bailable by default — that requires a hearing specifically to show the evidence against him isn't strong. Separately, the court gave him 10 days to explain why he shouldn't be preventively suspended while the trial runs.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So two separate motions moving at once — bail, and suspension.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Right, and evidence pre-marking keeps running on a rolling schedule through this week. The bail motion is the one to watch — if a plunder defendant this prominent gets bail, that's a genuinely different signal about how this case is likely to go than the arraignment alone told us.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Anything on the economy?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Barclays is now forecasting one more BSP hike, 25 basis points to 5.25%, in October — up from the current 5% set in August. Driver is September inflation, estimated at 6.5% in a BusinessWorld poll, the sixth straight month above the BSP's 3% ceiling, on oil prices and peso weakness.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the peso itself?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Closed Friday at 62.75 to the dollar — actually off the record weak print of 62.86 from two weeks ago, so a slight steadying, not a fresh record. PSEi fell 1.72% to a two-week low, but that's mostly the same Fed-hike whiplash we've already covered, not a new story on its own. Weather's quiet — no active PAGASA signal, just routine thunderstorm advisories up north.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two Mandarin words today, both built for the China story coming up — a fiscal hole that's getting deeper by policy design.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: First word: 不惜, bùxī. It means "not hesitate to," even at real cost — a formal, written-register word, 书面语, almost always paired with a word for the cost itself.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What does it pair with most often?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Most commonly 代价, "cost" or "price" — 不惜代价, "whatever the cost." Or 不惜一切, "at any cost, no matter what." It signals real commitment, even recklessness, not casual willingness.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Example: 一些地方政府不惜代价维持土地财政，即使收入已经大幅下降。("Some local governments won't hesitate to pay any cost to keep relying on land revenue, even as that revenue has fallen sharply.")

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second word — 权衡, quánhéng.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: "To weigh up," as in weighing pros and cons before a decision — also formal register, common in policy and finance writing. It's a verb, not a connective, but it's fully abstract — you're always weighing something against something else.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What does it collocate with?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 利弊, "pros and cons" — 权衡利弊. Or 得失, "gains and losses" — 权衡得失. Both are set phrases you'll see constantly in financial commentary.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Example: 北京必须权衡利弊，决定是继续收紧预售政策，还是放松以稳住地方财政。("Beijing has to weigh the pros and cons of whether to keep tightening presale policy or ease up to stabilize local government finances.") We'll hear both of these again in a moment.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 北京必须权衡利弊，因为卖地收入下降的速度比预期快得多。("Beijing has to weigh the pros and cons here, because land-sale revenue is falling faster than expected.") And there's a new number behind that sentence.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's the number?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Goldman Sachs just revised its estimate of the hit from Beijing's shift toward completed-home-only presales — now projecting a 30% cut to land-sale revenue nationwide, up from an earlier estimate of 20%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Why does requiring completed homes instead of presales hit land sales specifically?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Because it's cash-strapped developers who bid for new land, and forcing them to finish units before selling them ties up the capital they'd otherwise use to bid at the next auction. It's a policy-driven hit, not just a demand-driven one — Beijing chose this mechanism knowing it would slow land turnover.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And local governments depend on those land sales specifically.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Historically about 40% of local government revenue comes from land sales. Local government debt nationwide is already estimated near $18.9 trillion — roughly matching the size of the entire Chinese economy.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So this converts what looked like a developer liquidity problem into something structural.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Exactly the shift — 一些地方政府不惜代价维持土地财政，即使收入已经大幅下降。Some local governments won't hesitate to pay any cost to keep relying on land revenue, even as that revenue keeps falling. Beijing is simultaneously expanding central borrowing to backstop local governments, while the land-revenue base underneath keeps shrinking by policy design, not by accident.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Is there a way out of that loop, or is it just going to keep compounding?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The honest answer is Beijing has to actually choose — keep tightening the presale rules for financial-stability reasons and accept a smaller local-government revenue base permanently, or loosen the rules and accept the developer-leverage risk the reform was designed to fix in the first place. There's no version where they get both a stable land market and this reform intact.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Arts today leads with opera — a fresh production at the Paris Opera getting real notice this week.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: OperaWire's review, published the 17th — Rossini's "Il Barbiere di Siviglia" at Opéra Bastille. Conductor Jader Bignamini got singled out for a reading of the score OperaWire called "fluid, sparkling," and — this is the detail worth sitting with — "very Mozartian," for a score that's almost always played broader and brasher.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What does "Mozartian" actually mean for a Rossini score in practice?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Tighter ensemble balance, more restraint in the comic timing, less of the pure vocal-fireworks approach conductors usually lean on for Rossini specifically. It's a genuinely different interpretive choice, not just a well-executed standard reading.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the staging?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Damiano Michieletto's production, which is returning rather than new — sets Seville as a lived-in, playful contemporary city rather than a period postcard. The combination of an unusually restrained pit and a loose, contemporary stage is what's getting the attention.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: A second item — the Booker Prize shortlist comes out tomorrow.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The longlist, announced back in July, is unusually stacked — two former winners, Douglas Stuart for "John of John" and Marlon James for "The Disappearers," plus Elizabeth Strout for "The Things We Never Say."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Three big names on one longlist is rare.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Genuinely rare, and it's got people reading it as the judges deliberately rewarding risk this cycle rather than playing it safe with debut discoveries. We'll know tomorrow which of the three, if any, actually makes the cut.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Op-eds — and Jonathan Levin at Bloomberg Opinion is calling out something uncomfortable about three central banks at once.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: His piece, published Sunday: the US, UK, and Japan are all simultaneously talking tough on inflation while quietly leaning against rising long-bond yields — buybacks, dovish signaling, jawboning. Accelerator and brake at the same time, and none of them are taking the politically hard step of actually shrinking their deficits.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Steelman it.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a fair diagnosis — you can't credibly fight inflation while also working to suppress the market signal, long yields, that's supposed to discipline fiscal behavior. Doing both at once is exactly the kind of muddle that erodes central-bank credibility over time.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the counter?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The piece treats yield-curve-control-lite as pure dysfunction, but there's a reasonable case it's a rational bridge — governments facing simultaneous debt-rollover walls and growth-sensitive electorates might genuinely be better off managing yields short-term while inflation cools on its own, rather than forcing a fiscal crisis to prove a point. And lumping the US, UK, and Japan into one "muddle" overstates how similar their actual situations are.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second piece — Tyler Austin Harper in The Atlantic, and this one's personal.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Harper just quit a tenure-track post at Bates College. His cover essay, "Confessions of a Token Black Professor," argues elite campuses institutionalized a moralized, activist-driven version of DEI between 2020 and 2023 that administrators used less to fix actual inequity than to manage reputational risk — and it flattened him personally into a symbolic role.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Steelman that one.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a credible first-person account of a real dynamic — plenty of people in academia have quietly described exactly this tension between symbolic representation and substantive support, and Harper's willing to put his name on it after leaving, which costs him something.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And the counter-take?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Chronicle Review's response is the sharp one — Harper generalizes from one small liberal-arts college's specific excesses to "American academia" writ large, and a personal disillusionment memoir framed as structural diagnosis is exactly the kind of piece that gets weaponized by a broader anti-DEI backlash that has its own bad-faith actors. Both sides are already using it as ammunition rather than sitting with it as analysis.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which of the two lands harder this week?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Harper piece, honestly, because it's forcing a conversation people have mostly had privately into public view — the Levin piece is sharp but describes a dynamic close-watchers already assumed was happening.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: We'll close today in San Jose, with a 47-year-old named Justin Buzzard.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What's his story?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Buzzard's a pastor, a church founder, and a father of three — and back as a teenager, an injury ended his football career before it really started. Nearly 30 years later, he walked on as a freshman defensive lineman at San Jose City College.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: At 47.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: At 47 — and it's not a ceremonial thing. He actually played his first live snaps August 29th against College of the Redwoods, in a real game, against actual 18-year-olds.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: What made him go back now, after three decades?

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: By all accounts, just unfinished business — the injury took the decision away from him at 17, and this was him finally making the choice for himself, three kids and a congregation later.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Clean story, no caveat needed there.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: None at all — just someone deciding it's never actually too late to finish what got taken from you.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's The Morning Commute for Monday, September 21st.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Have a good one — we'll see you tomorrow.
